blocks.p: Somewhere in the dark ahead, a printer breathed out a page.

blocks.cap: The way down to the registry floor

blocks.p: The registry floor was two levels below the dying plant and the kind man. Rei went down by the back stairs, because the lifts had cameras and the stairs, as far as he could see, did not.

The stairwell was painted the same grey as the outside of the building. Each landing had a fire extinguisher, a green running-man exit sign and a small window of frosted glass that let in a dull white light. On the first landing down the air was still warm. On the second it was not. The sounds of the building fell away above him, the phones, the ticket machine, the quiet voices. By the bottom of the stairs Rei could hear only his own breathing and his shoes on the concrete, and his breath had started to show faintly in front of his face, in August. At the bottom there was a heavy door with a card reader. He held up the borrowed pass. The reader thought about it for a pause long enough to make his scalp prickle. Then it decided that he was allowed.

Inside, the cold was no longer a thread. It filled the whole room, the way weather fills a valley. Rows of grey filing cabinets stood in the half-light like people who had been waiting a long time. The only sound was the printer he had heard through the floor. It was a single machine at the end of the central aisle, breathing out a page every few minutes into a tray already thick with pages.

He walked toward it past drawers labelled in handwriting too even to be human. As he walked, he understood that this was not a place where records were stored. It was a place where records were kept alive. They were fed, certified and renewed, so that the people they described could be quietly held in whatever state the building wanted them in.
The page in the tray was his brother.

doc.title: Civil Veil Division. Registry. Status Verification

blocks.p: The page beneath it was the same. And the one below that, the same, and the same. A stack of identical certificates went back through the days in layers. Each one was a small official act of looking at an empty chair and writing present.

He lifted the stack, and the dates ran backward under his thumb. Three days. A week. Two weeks. Then the pattern broke. The oldest pages in the tray were different. They were not automatic. They had been signed, once, by a person, before the machine took over. And the person who started the lie had written a short note in the margin of the first one, with an initial. No machine would ever write a note like that. The ink had gone the brown of old blood.
Per consultation. Y. He asked so little.

Rei stood among the cold cabinets with the proof in his hands, and he saw how the whole thing worked. Someone had started this by hand. Someone had sat at a desk in late July and made the first false certificate himself, willingly, gratefully. A consultation had asked very little of him, and had given him, Rei could only guess, something he wanted very much. Then he had taught the machine to do the rest. He had set it to renew Gin every morning at six, and then walked away into a personal leave for his health. And the form had been filing itself ever since, keeping Rei's brother present in the only record that could ever have declared him gone.

He should have left. He photographed the signed pages, and he should have turned for the door. Instead the cold pulled him sideways, down a row he had no reason to enter, the way grief pulls a hand toward a drawer it should not open.

blocks.cap: The older cabinets of the registry, labelled with names

blocks.p: The cabinets here were older. Their labels were names, and the names had small coloured tabs. After the third one he understood the colours. Green meant active. Green was the lie. There were more green tabs in this row than any building should need. A whole quiet harvest of people the registry was certifying as present, each with a tray, each with a printer somewhere bringing them back to life on paper at six in the morning. Beside each of the oldest, in the same brown ink, was the same note. Per consultation. Y.

The thing that had done this had a name on the streets of Kita, though Rei did not learn it until later. People there called it the Healer. It had been busy for much longer than Gin's three days. It had asked so little of so many, and filed every favour in a room two floors below the kindest man Rei had ever met.

He thought of the secret page in Gin's book, the one with the heaviest stamp. Component One. Catalogue. Identification and detailed profiling of all practitioners at Level 3 and above. At the kitchen table it had been words on paper. Now he was standing inside it. This was what a catalogue looked like when someone had their hand on the drawer. A name, a tab, a status, a printer. The building did not need to find a person to hold him. It only needed to keep writing down that he was where it wanted him to be.

At the end of the row the labels reached the U's. He found the drawer before he had decided to look for it. UEDERA. Inside there was one folder, with a green tab and his brother's name on it. It was thick with six years of assessments, and every one of them read C.

There was no second folder. Rei went through the drawer twice with cold fingers, and then the drawers on either side of it, in case a card had been put in the wrong place. There was nothing with his name on it anywhere. He remembered a line from the preface to Gin's Chapter Four, written on a Wednesday when they had eaten ramen and Rei had fallen asleep on the couch. Rei's file in the CVD system does not exist. He has never been formally assessed. He had read it as a fact. Standing in this room, he read it again as a piece of work. Somebody had kept that drawer empty for nineteen years, in a building whose whole purpose was to fill it.
He closed the drawer very gently, as if the empty space inside it could be bruised.

One drawer was already open. Rei had not opened it. It stuck an inch out into the aisle, as if someone had just looked something up. The file inside was not green, and it was not under any name he knew. It was an index, a list of the registry's own lists. And the entry it lay open at was not a person. It was a seat.

The same words. The same even, machine-like hand. But here they described a seat, not a man. Thirteen registers, Rei remembered, and here was the thirteenth, written up like a chair in some other office entirely. The building was keeping it vacant the same way it kept his brother active. It wrote the condition it wanted down every morning, again and again, until the truth gave up arguing.

Rei looked at the word null-emotive. It meant, as far as he could tell, a register with no feeling in it at all. He thought of the Kuroda house, and the fold, and the word that had settled in him there with no pity in it. Duty. The building had a name for this seat, and it was the wrong one. Nobody here had looked closely enough to see what kind of chair it was. Looking at it, he understood that he had walked out of his brother's disappearance and into the edge of something bigger that used the same pen. Whatever was thinning the wall between the worlds was also a clerk. It did its largest work on the smallest pieces of paper.

The cold sharpened, the way a held breath sharpens just before it is let go. He became aware that the open drawer had not been left open by chance. It had been left open for him. The pass that should not exist had not been a simple mistake. It had walked him down two floors and along one row to a drawer that stuck out into the aisle at exactly the height of his eyes. And somewhere a kind, busy thing was watching what he would do with an empty seat it had gone to the trouble of showing him.

He did the only thing he knew how to do. He breathed out and let his attention go loose, and he looked at the drawer the way a bored intern looks at a drawer. It did not help. Whatever was watching had not come to measure his rank. It had come to see what he wanted.

The favour had found him. It had not asked for anything yet. For now it was only letting him read. It was letting him feel the link between a brother kept present and a seat kept empty. And it was trusting, the way it trusted everyone, that once he saw how little it asked, he would want very much to be helped.

He came up out of the building into the full weight of the August morning, and the city did not know. That was the thing that nearly took his legs out from under him on the steps of the Directorate. Tokyo was going about Obon. Strings of lanterns hung between the lampposts for the dead who were allowed to come home. A woman was arranging chrysanthemums in a bucket outside a konbini, the white and yellow flowers people take to graves. A child was being walked to the swimming pool with a towel around his neck. And two floors below all of it a machine was certifying Rei's brother alive on a schedule, and none of these warm, ordinary, breathing people would ever take a ticket in that line.

He had the photographs in his phone. He had the pass on its lanyard, which he had not given back. He stood in the heat, shivering. The cold had marked him as a stranger, and he carried that with him now, wherever he went.

The cicadas ground on. Somewhere over the rooftops a temple bell rang slowly. People say that sound carries to the other side. Rei thought about which side his brother was on. Not dead. The registry insisted he was not dead. Only active. Only present. Only renewed at six each morning by a form that had learned to file itself, from the moment a tired official decided a favour had asked so little of him.

He thought about Sekine's dying plant and the chair with no one in it. He thought about a row of green tabs and a drawer that had opened itself to show him an empty seat. And he understood that the briefing they had kept quiet was the truest document in the building. It was not a thing said. It was a thing carefully not said, an absence managed so smoothly that the only way to see it was to become the kind of person who notices what is missing. Over three days in his brother's cold home, he had become that person.

He took out the lanyard one more time, there on the steps, in the lantern light and the heat, and looked at the pass that carried the authority of a man who was not gone. He could give it back. He could walk into the ordinary morning and let the form file itself for ever.

He put it back in his pocket, next to Gin's useless key. He would come back tomorrow, before six, and be standing at the printer when it tried to renew his brother. He would see for himself whether an absence that had been written down could also be crossed out. Or whether the only thing his borrowed key really opened was the next room in a trap. A trap that had been certifying him, too, as present and accounted for, from the moment he took a ticket.
